query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A simple fluorine‐based surface treatment applied to an aluminum-containing refractory high‐entropy alloy will promote the rapid formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale during high‐temperature exposure, thereby significantly reducing oxygen uptake compared to untreated alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractive high‐entropy alloy (e.g., one containing Al along with refractory elements such as Nb, Ta, and Hf) with its native, unmodified surface.
generation.intervention: Application of a fluorine-based surface treatment (e.g., by spraying or dipping in a low-concentration NH4F/HF aqueous solution).
generation.conditions: The treated alloy is exposed to flowing dry air at an elevated temperature of about 1100 °C, with isothermal oxidation for up to 200 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: The fluorine species modify the surface chemistry so that reactive Al preferentially oxidizes to form a dense, continuous and adherent Al2O3 film that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Fluorine treatment promotes selective oxidation by activating Al oxidation. At high temperature, volatile aluminum fluorides form and then decompose in the presence of oxygen to yield an adherent alumina layer. This shift in oxidation kinetics suppresses the rapid formation and growth of less-protective oxides (such as TiO2 or mixed oxide scales) and limits oxygen ingress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated RHEA specimens, the fluorine-treated alloys are predicted to have a markedly lower mass gain (potentially a reduction of over 50% in weight gain during oxidation) and a more uniform, adherent Al2O3 scale that improves long-term oxidation resistance under extreme temperatures.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys which, while mechanically robust, form mixed, less-protective oxide scales with higher oxygen uptake during long-term high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to apply to RHEAs that include a sufficient aluminum content to form stable Al2O3 and under dry air conditions at temperatures near 1100 °C; it might not be effective for compositions with very low Al or in atmospheres with moisture or reactive species that could interfere with Al2O3 formation.
generation.uncertainty: While the fluorine effect has been demonstrated in TiAl alloys (evidence from PMC9030595) and the importance of forming protective alumina scales in RHEAs has been stressed (e.g., in PMC6513993 and PMC10142552), it is uncertain how the fluorine species interact with the unique multicomponent matrix of RHEAs. The extent to which the kinetics of Al oxidation are modified in these complex alloys remains to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from an aluminum-containing refractory high-entropy alloy. Subject one set to the proposed fluorine-based surface treatment by spraying with a controlled NH4F solution, while leaving the other set untreated. Expose both sets to isothermal oxidation in flowing dry air at 1100 °C for 200 hours inside a thermogravimetric apparatus. After exposure, characterize mass gain, surface oxide scale morphology (using SEM/EDS), and measure the continuity and composition of the oxide layers (via XRD).
measurements: Mass gain per unit area over time (TGA data).
Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (cross-sectional SEM).
Phase composition of the oxide scale (XRD/EDS analysis).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fluorine-treated alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant lower mass gain (e.g., at least 50% reduction) compared to the untreated alloy, or if the oxide scale does not predominantly consist of a continuous and adherent Al2O3 layer, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2, which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. In-depth analyses of the anti-oxidation behavior and structure of γ-TiAl alloys are of great significant for their maintenance and repair in engineering applications. In this work, fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys and fluorine-treated oxidized specimens with artificial defects were prepared by isothermal oxidation treatment at 1000 °C. Several characterization methods, including SEM, EDS, XRD and TEM, were used to evaluate the surface microstructure of the fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys and fluorine-treated oxidized specimens with artificial defects. The results indicate that the fluorine promoted the formation of an outer protective film of Al2O3, which significantly improved the oxidation resistance. The microcracks of oxidized specimens with the artificial defects provided a rapid diffusion passage for Ti and O elements during the 1000 °C/2 h isothermal oxidation treatment process, resulting in the quick growth of TiO2 toward the outside. The fine Al2O3 constituted a continuous film after the 1000 °C/100 h isothermal oxidation treatment.
